lines.text: A small island at the crossroads of the seas, that turned itself into one of the richest places on Earth. This is the story of Singapore.
In the thirteen hundreds a Malay kingdom called Singapura stood on the island, remembered in the Malay Annals.
Centuries later the British official Stamford Raffles saw the island's place on the trade routes, and in 1819 set up a trading post.
So modern Singapore began, a free port at the tip of the Malay Peninsula.
Its harbour on the Strait of Malacca grew into one of the busiest ports in the world, full of Chinese, Malay and Indian traders.
In 1826 Singapore, Penang and Malacca were joined as the British colony of the Straits Settlements.
In 1859 the Botanic Gardens were founded. Rubber trees for Malaya were first grown there, and the gardens are now a World Heritage site.
The Raffles Hotel opened in 1887, a grand colonial hotel where the Singapore Sling was invented.
In 1905 the city's first university began, today among the best in Asia.
Lee Kuan Yew, born in 1923, would become the first prime minister, and lead Singapore through independence and rapid growth.
Goh Chok Tong would follow him as prime minister, from 1990 to 2004.
In February 1942 the British garrison surrendered to Japan, Britain's worst defeat of the war.
The occupiers then killed tens of thousands of Chinese men in the Sook Ching massacre.
Lee Kuan Yew's son, Lee Hsien Loong, would later lead the country for twenty years.
In 1960 a housing board was set up, and over the years it built flats for most of Singapore's people.
In 1963 Singapore joined the new Federation of Malaysia. Two years later it was expelled.
Its national airline took to the skies, and would become famous for its service.
On the ninth of August 1965 Singapore became an independent nation, small, alone, and determined.
Lawrence Wong, born in 1972, would become prime minister in 2024.
In 1981 Changi Airport opened, often named the best airport in the world.
In 2008 Formula One held its first ever night race, through Singapore's city streets.
Two years later Marina Bay Sands opened, three towers joined at the top by a park in the sky.
And in 2012 Gardens by the Bay opened beside it, with giant glass houses and towers shaped like trees.
From a trading post to a garden city, Singapore shows how far a small island can go.
